title: 2008 AMC 10A Problem 3
statement: For the positive integer \(n,\) let \(\langle n \rangle\) denote the sum of all the positive divisors of \(n\) with the exception of \(n\) itself. For example, \(\langle 4 \rangle = 1 + 2 = 3\) and \(\langle 12 \rangle = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 16.\) What is \(\langle\langle\langle 6 \rangle\rangle\rangle?\)

solutions.text:
The positive divisors of \(6\) other than \(6\) are \(1, 2,\) and \(3,\) so \(\langle 6 \rangle = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.\)

Since applying the operation to \(6\) again returns \(6,\) we get \(\langle\langle\langle 6 \rangle\rangle\rangle = 6.\)

(A number equal to the sum of its proper divisors is called a perfect number, and \(6\) is the smallest.)

Thus, the correct answer is A.
hints: \(\langle 6 \rangle\) is the sum of the divisors of \(6\) other than \(6\)
Compute \(\langle 6 \rangle\) first; the result feeds back into the same operation
